newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Economic rebound not alleviating Argentine deficit.
newsitem.headline: Economic rebound not alleviating Argentine deficit.

text.p: The rebound in Argentina's economy is not being reflected in the level of tax revenues and is not helping alleviate the pressure on the public deficit, analysts said.
They added that if the trend continued in 1997, it could derail public finances and oblige a renegotiation of the terms of Argentina's deal with the International Monetary Fund.

"Clearly the tax collected in November was very mediocre; maybe the domestic market is depressed or the economy is not growing as fast as it seems," said Daniel Artana, an economist at private consultancy FIEL. In November, a month that saw a rise in fuel taxes, total tax collection amounted to $3.71 billion compared with an official forecast of $3.85 billion.

And though the tax collected in November was 4.6 percent higher than in November 1995, analysts had been expecting a strong rise in revenue in line with the 7.5 percent economic growth expected for the fourth quarter. Gross domestic product growth is seen at 3.5 percent for this year as a whole.

"Tax collection is not good; this level of collection is compatible with an annual deficit of $6.0 billion, such as I expect in 1996 and 1997," said Jose Luis Espert, director of consultants Econometrica.

"With the low rate of capital inflows compared with the surge between 1991 and 1994 -- a period in which Argentine growth was 8.9 percent annually -- if the government's inability to save persists, private savings growth of 4-5.0 percent cannot be sustained in 1997," he added.
The government agreed with the IMF on a deficit of $4.5 billion in 1997, including interest payments on public debt but excluding capital income such as privatizations.

"The level of tax collection is not terrible but below expectations," said Jose Rutman, an economist at consultancy Broda y Asociados, underlining disappointment that the new fuel tax did not have a strong impact on revenues.
"Tax collection is growing but it is insufficient to reduce the fiscal deficit, and this is within the context of a strong rebound in growth," he added.

A more pessimistic analysis came from Rodolfo Rossi, former head of the Central Bank. "The economic rebound is very tenuous, consumption is stagnant, and fiscal pressure is too high to expect much more from tax collection," he said.
Still there was a rise in income tax revenue in November to $674 million, 21.7 percent higher than in November last year, although the total weighting of income tax is low.

Since the second half of 1994, the public sector deficit has been on an upward trajectory, obliging the government to renegotiate its agreed deficit with the International Monetary Fund for this year to $6.0 billion.

And according to analysts the outlook for 1997 is not different, with the measures agreed with the IMF looking to a deficit of $4.5 billion seen incompatible with the levels of tax collection and the planned increase in public expenditure.
"I easily predict a deficit of $7.0 billion (in 1997)," said Rossi, compared with an estimate by Broda y Asociados of $6.0 billion.

Analysts were especially surprised by the low level of domestic value added tax collected by the DGI tax service, which was 2.1 percent lower than in November 1995, in contrast with a 27 percent rise in VAT collections by customs.
"The rebound can be seen in imports but internal demand is still at very depressed levels and no improvements can be seen in the fight against tax evasion," said Espert.
Artana suggested the low VAT revenue could have something to do with technical adjustments by firms that decided to make use of previous tax credits. -- Buenos Aires Newsroom, +541 318-0654
